OGIES STANDOFF

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Despite our expose of the structural damage, noise and dust Glencore's coal mining has caused in Ogies, Glencore's operations have expanded and the residents are desperate.

Unique Selling Point:
While the human rights lawyers attempt to get a court date to have the problems aired in court, it appears that Glencore has rapidly expanded their blasting on the edge of the town of Ogies -- making breathing and sleep virtually impossible.

When the community protested against the dust last week -- they found themselves on the receiving end of police action.

The community has been at logger heads with the mine for a long time now. As a result of many dissatisfactory engagements with some representatives of the mine, they took the step of protesting and drafting a memorandum to hand to Glencore.

One of the leaders who has charges against him, Joseph Zikhali wants the community of Ogies and Phola to be the first group of people that benefit from the mining activities.

“Charity must begin at home before the mine can look elsewhere. I want the charges against me to be dropped as I am not a criminal I am simply fighting for our rights. Until such time where people will be employed, compensated and benefit from the mine. We will not rest."



Summary:
Many of the issues the community is protesting, have not shifted in years. The standoff with Glencore seems deeper than ever.

MEMORANDUM DEMANDS:
1) Inadequate and unfair economic exclusion of the hosting community and its residents in the continued mining activities of the mine.
2) Families relocated to Makause who still do not have water and electricity supply.
3) Compensation for forced removals and the relocation of graves without following traditional customs.
4) The mine and all its major contractors to demonstrate their local employment and skills development statistics, local Small Medium and Micro-Enterprises (SMME’s) that they are developing and are currently contracted directly with the mine or any of its major contractors. Show their local socio economic development initiatives.
5) Demand that all criminal charges and the court interdict against any of their leaders resulting from their many attempts to raise their concerns be immediately withdrawn.
6) Families relocated in order to allow for mining operations to take place be compensated and collectively explore a way in which they can benefit directly in the continued mining activities.


Further information:
BACKGROUND FROM PAST STORY:
Guest house owners Annemarie and Mike Muller (late 50s) permanently carry around tissues -- but their constant health problems are the least of their worries -- what gets to them is that they may never get back the R6-million that they sunk into developing two guest houses in Ogies, after cashing in their pensions to invest in the town.
With mines booming around the town and another application pending that will take mining to within a few hundred metres of their yard, they should have made in killing in the business guest trade. In stead the town is slowly killing them.
Their home and guest houses are cracking from the constant and untimely dynamite explosions to prepare the way for mining and the heavy-duty dragline crunches away day and night, disturbing the rest of residents and visitors. A thick layer of black dust hangs in the air all the time.
The people of Ogies have roped in human rights lawyer Zehir Omar to help them fight three mines in their area (GLENCORE, ANGLO AMERICAN and SHAFT32) on human rights grounds.
The DISRTESSED MINING COMMUNITY OF OGIES COMMITTEE that's been founded between the town and township, claims their right to a safe and clean environment is being destroyed, without them ever having been consulted on what was to come...now they sit with houses cracked and banks unwilling to touch the area, so they cannot sell up and leave.


OGIES' LEGAL CASE:
Two local doctors are willing to stick their necks out to confirm that a rising incidence of respiratory diseases in the area can be attributed to the intense pollution by coal dust.

The group has had some minor success in court already this year when they managed to get a South Gauteng High Court innterdict to stop Glencore from privatising a public road for their own use...a move that would have cut off the town's access to the main school.

Omar feels that the community's problems would be completely addressed and solved if only the Department of Mineral Resources would send an inspector to the area to look at the residents complaints. Having got nowhere with getting said inspector to the area, he's approached the Public Protector (that office should really be willing and able to investigate the abuse or neglect of state institutions to enforce residents' complaints)...but the Public Protector dismissed Omar and Ogies and threaten to lump them with costs, should they pursue the matter.

For their part, all three mines deny any wrongdoing and have been fighting Omar in court.

Glencore aims to mine an area of 113m2 for another 22 years -- it denies that it's encroaching on the town...we would have to get independent expert opinion but it certainly LOOKS to the naked eye that they're closer than the 1000m buffer zone they should be.

I want to pull the focus a bit wider -- 67% of Mpumalanga is now covered by open cast coal mining -- this has cut the production of maize by a million tonnes.

According to an often-quoted study by the Northwest University on behalf of West European governments that are considering whether to re-open certain mining areas in Europe, Witbank and surroundings -- up to and including areas like Ogies, are now THE most polluted in the world of any mining area that's been the subject of study.

I want to investigate problems with breathing and water -- in Witbank (provincial capital, half hour away from Ogies) I have reports/case studies of black lung/mining tuberculosis in people who've never mined, but who live right next to mine dumps.

This is all happening in a context where the area has already paid a heavy price for virtually unrestricted coal mining -- Anglo is paying a fortune to rehabilitate the town's drinking water and there have long been sink holes and burning earth from old and abandoned coal mines.

Press Release:


Ogies Standoff
Structural damage, untimely blasting and black dust - coal mining is encroaching ever closer to homes in Ogies in Mpumalanga and pleas for intervention seem to be falling on deaf ears. In a desperate attempt to put an end to the coal mine blasting, fed-up residents with damaged homes and poor health, take on major mining companies. Carte Blanche returns to Ogies to investigate how the lives of those affected have deteriorated rapidly.


Script:


SCRIPT: OGIES STANDOFF
PRODUCERS: Anna-Maria van Niekerk & Marzanne van den Berg
PRESENTER: Macfarlane Moleli
TX: 11 March 2018
DURATION: 8 minutes

VO: On the Highveld coal belt, emotions are running high.

MACFARLANE LINK: Just six months ago we reported on the alleged human rights violations by mines in the town of Ogies in Mpumalanga and now the standoff intensifies.

VO: When Carte Blanche was here in August last year, a LOCAL COMMUNITY FORUM was preparing to take mining company Glencore to court over their Constitutional right to an environment that’s not harmful. Anne-Marie Muller is secretary of the Distressed Mining Community of Ogies Forum.

(STRAP: Carte Blanche, August 2017) DEREK WATTS: What is it like when there’s a big blast here?
ANNE-MARIE MULLER, SECRETARY: DISTRESSED MINING COMMUNITY OF OGIES FORUM: It’s frightening sometimes. You can feel the vibration coming. The lights here it starts swinging, the windows it’s rattling -- it’s terrible.

VO: Anglo American and South32 also mine coal nearby but it’s Glencore that the Forum holds responsible for the damage to homes and making their lives unbearable. Glencore disputes this.

(STRAP: Carte Blanche, August 2017) ANNE-MARIE MULLER, SECRETARY: DISTRESSED MINING COMMUNITY OF OGIES FORUM: Five years ago, you heard the blasting, but you never feel it so with impact, but the past four…three, four years, it’s really getting terrible.

VO: Anne-Marie and her husband Adriaan own a guest house and creche -- they were shocked in December to discover Glencore’s staff digging heaps of topsoil in a wide stretch of land behind their property all the way to the church a few blocks away.

ANNE-MARIE MULLER, SECRETARY: DISTRESSED MINING COMMUNITY OF OGIES FORUM: The new expansion started right here at the back of my preschool, right at the back of some of… one of the churches here.

VO: Tebello Setenane is a teacher at the Muller’s creche and lives in a back room nearby. Machines grinding into the night are causing her 7-year old son great distress.

TEBELLO SETENANE, RESIDENT: Sometimes it’s hard for us to sleep according to the noise that we heard from the trucks.
MACFARLANE MOLELI: Very close to your yard.
TEBELLO SETENANE, RESIDENT: The dust in my house if we because the heaps of the soil is just nearby here and when the… when the wind blows…
MACFARLANE MOLELI: All of that dust comes into the house...
TEBELLO SETENANE, RESIDENT: No, you can not clean up that house.

VO: A block away from the church is Joseph Zikhali’s house. In January, this crack appeared.

JOSEPH ZIKHALI, RESIDENT: When they blast, you can forget about it, that’s when more houses get cracks. There’s many cracks … and also the kids are suffering with the noise of the machines.

VO: Glencore declined our invitation to come on camera. They confirmed they would start blasting and excavating near the town at the end of March. They’re busy moving topsoil into raised banks to buffer against the noise. After our last story, the Mullers discovered some paperwork about mining plans for nearby farms. They never realised it would be so close to them.

ADRIAAN MULLER, GUESTHOUSE AND CRÈCHE OWNER: Nowhere in this document it states anything about Ogies. It’s portion this, portion this, portion this. So nobody understand where they’re going to mine.

VO: Published in 2015, Glencore’s Environmental Impact Assessment report lists the risks of pollution, discomfort and damage and suggests that those living within a kilometre of mining may have to be resettled. The Forum’s attorney is Zehir Omar.

ZEHIR OMAR, ATTORNEY: This impact assessment report was submitted and Glencore was authorised to expand its mining operations. The EIA, itself, records the enormous harm to the environment, to human health, safety of human beings…

VO: Glencore, in a joint venture with African Rainbow Minerals, can mine up to the town borders and says it complies with its environmental plans. But residents say it’s unbearable to live so close to mining machines that crunch till 10 at night and start up at sunrise.

MACFARLANE LINK: With the mining operations getting closer and closer to the people’s homes, there aren’t many options for the people of Ogies in Mpumalanga. It’s either they move, or fight… but moving without compensation is not an option, so the fight is on.

ZEHIR OMAR, ATTORNEY: Go to the people. Pay them fair compensation and talk to them with the aim of moving. This is expropriation using coercion through mining.

ADRIAAN MULLER, GUESTHOUSE AND CRÈCHE OWNER: Buy us out, we go. Otherwise, we’re going to stop Glencore’s new operations, we’re going to stop them.

VO: Glencore insists it’s compliant on every level. Locals say Glencore just ticks legal boxes without meaningful engagement or building a mutually beneficial relationship with them.

JOSEPH ZIKHALI, RESIDENT: We keep on fighting with this Glencore. The main thing it’s the production. They don’t worry about our lives.

VO: Feeling the mine disregards them, Zikhali and some of his supporters marched to the mine and handed a memorandum of grievances to management in February. Steven Mhlanga joined that march.

MACFARLANE MOLELI: Is there absolutely no engagement happening between you and the mine to try and resolve these issues?

STEVEN MHLANGA, RESIDENT: There are forums, but it’s a lip service that they give to us. They just want to come there and just speak and speak, but nothing happens. It’s … no results.

VO: Mhlanga, like many locals, used to live on farms that were taken over by the mines. Mhlanga and his grandparents were relocated to Phola, a township to the north of Ogies, three years ago.

STEVEN MHLANGA, RESIDENT: There’s other cracks this side. This solar is not working.

VO: Like many others, Mhlanga feels they got tiny, shoddily built houses and empty promises.

STEVEN MHLANGA, RESIDENT: Here we’re just suffering more. They just brought us more, more, more deep into poverty.

VO: Glencore says building inspectors signed off on all the houses they built. Without ESKOM power to the area, Glencore says each house has a solar geyser and gas stove; plus municipal water and rainwater tanks. Protesters feel the mine made empty promises to get the community’s support.

JOSEPH ZIKHALI, RESIDENT: In the memorandum we mention quite of things, the skills development, because our community they are not working in this mine. Our town -- you can see how many potholes are here, we can’t do nothing, because we don’t have nothing. Glencore is here, they don’t help us with nothing.

VO: Glencore says most of the mine’s employees live within 50 km of the mine and they prioritise hiring locals. About 18% are from Ogies and Phola and 67% from Emalahleni, 40 km away.

MACFARLANE MOLELI: So you people are ready to work, you just want opportunities?
STEVEN MHLANGA, RESIDENT: We want opportunities and then make our lives better.

VO: Glencore hit back at protesters, getting an urgent interdict to stop the group from obstructing the mine’s business. It said they caused “irreparable harm” when they blocked the mine entrance and threw stones. Zikhali’s due back in court in May to say why the interdict should not be made permanent.

VO: In January Glencore suffered a blow in the Land Claims Court when it tried to urgently evict the last few families from GGV Village to Phola. The land now belongs to the mine but the people have lived there for decades.

ZEHIR OMAR, ATTORNEY: How do you order a whole community living in a rural community to supplant themselves into an urban setup? It’s a small matchbox house. You are imposing a huge trauma on men, women and children.

VO: The families say they will go if Glencore buys them a similar plot. The Land Claims Court agreed it was dangerous to live so close to mining, but Glencore must go through the usual legal eviction process in terms of the Extension of Security of Tenure Act.

MACFARLANE LINK: The people of this village have won the battle to stay here for now. They refused to relocate to a township -- a life to which they are not accustomed. But how long can they hold onto their property with mining operations just at their doorstep?

VO: Glencore says it now uses electronic blasting, which limits noise and ground vibration. But residents say it does little to alleviate the noise of machinery and dust.

ANNE-MARIE MULLER, SECRETARY: DISTRESSED MINING COMMUNITY OF OGIES FORUM: ...it does affect you, because some of the people, they start complaining, they’re got running noses, they got headaches... There’s children staying here that some medical reports says it’s air pollution that they got this allergic to the eyes, to the nose, kept with… they’ve got… they’re constantly sick. The mine says there is nothing that can make you sick.

VO: The residents’ forum now waits for a court date to present their complaints to a judge.


PROMOS
10 secs
VO: It’s high noon in Ogies in Mpumalanga, as residents resort to violent protest and court action to battle the coal mining encroaching on their town.

15 secs
VO: Digging in their heels to preserve their way of life, a small community in Mpumalanga is taking on a coal mining giant. How long can they hold out?
ZEHIR OMAR, ATTORNEY: How do you order a whole community living in a rural community to supplant themselves into an urban setup?

15 secs
VO: With the dust and noise of coal mining operations now just a few hundred metres away from their homes, residents of Ogies in Mpumalanga are fed up.
ADRIAAN MULLER: Buy us out, we go. Otherwise, we’re going to stop Glencore’s new operations, we’re going to stop them.

Press Release: Ogies Standoff Structural damage, untimely blasting and black dust - coal mining is encroaching ever closer to homes in Ogies in Mpumalanga and pleas for intervention seem to be falling on deaf ears. In a desperate attempt to put an end to the coal mine blasting, fed-up residents with damaged homes and poor health, take on major mining companies. Carte Blanche returns to Ogies to investigate how the lives of those affected have deteriorated rapidly. Script: SCRIPT: OGIES STANDOFF PRODUCERS: Anna-Maria van Niekerk & Marzanne van den Berg PRESENTER: Macfarlane Moleli TX: 11 March 2018 DURATION: 8 minutes VO: On the Highveld coal belt, emotions are running high. MACFARLANE LINK: Just six months ago we reported on the alleged human rights violations by mines in the town of Ogies in Mpumalanga and now the standoff intensifies. VO: When Carte Blanche was here in August last year, a LOCAL COMMUNITY FORUM was preparing to take mining company Glencore to court over their Constitutional right to an environment that’s not harmful. Anne-Marie Muller is secretary of the Distressed Mining Community of Ogies Forum. (STRAP: Carte Blanche, August 2017) DEREK WATTS: What is it like when there’s a big blast here? ANNE-MARIE MULLER, SECRETARY: DISTRESSED MINING COMMUNITY OF OGIES FORUM: It’s frightening sometimes. You can feel the vibration coming. The lights here it starts swinging, the windows it’s rattling -- it’s terrible. VO: Anglo American and South32 also mine coal nearby but it’s Glencore that the Forum holds responsible for the damage to homes and making their lives unbearable. Glencore disputes this. (STRAP: Carte Blanche, August 2017) ANNE-MARIE MULLER, SECRETARY: DISTRESSED MINING COMMUNITY OF OGIES FORUM: Five years ago, you heard the blasting, but you never feel it so with impact, but the past four…three, four years, it’s really getting terrible. VO: Anne-Marie and her husband Adriaan own a guest house and creche -- they were shocked in December to discover Glencore’s staff digging heaps of topsoil in a wide stretch of land behind their property all the way to the church a few blocks away. ANNE-MARIE MULLER, SECRETARY: DISTRESSED MINING COMMUNITY OF OGIES FORUM: The new expansion started right here at the back of my preschool, right at the back of some of… one of the churches here. VO: Tebello Setenane is a teacher at the Muller’s creche and lives in a back room nearby. Machines grinding into the night are causing her 7-year old son great distress. TEBELLO SETENANE, RESIDENT: Sometimes it’s hard for us to sleep according to the noise that we heard from the trucks. MACFARLANE MOLELI: Very close to your yard. TEBELLO SETENANE, RESIDENT: The dust in my house if we because the heaps of the soil is just nearby here and when the… when the wind blows… MACFARLANE MOLELI: All of that dust comes into the house... TEBELLO SETENANE, RESIDENT: No, you can not clean up that house. VO: A block away from the church is Joseph Zikhali’s house. In January, this crack appeared. JOSEPH ZIKHALI, RESIDENT: When they blast, you can forget about it, that’s when more houses get cracks. There’s many cracks … and also the kids are suffering with the noise of the machines. VO: Glencore declined our invitation to come on camera. They confirmed they would start blasting and excavating near the town at the end of March. They’re busy moving topsoil into raised banks to buffer against the noise. After our last story, the Mullers discovered some paperwork about mining plans for nearby farms. They never realised it would be so close to them. ADRIAAN MULLER, GUESTHOUSE AND CRÈCHE OWNER: Nowhere in this document it states anything about Ogies. It’s portion this, portion this, portion this. So nobody understand where they’re going to mine. VO: Published in 2015, Glencore’s Environmental Impact Assessment report lists the risks of pollution, discomfort and damage and suggests that those living within a kilometre of mining may have to be resettled. The Forum’s attorney is Zehir Omar. ZEHIR OMAR, ATTORNEY: This impact assessment report was submitted and Glencore was authorised to expand its mining operations. The EIA, itself, records the enormous harm to the environment, to human health, safety of human beings… VO: Glencore, in a joint venture with African Rainbow Minerals, can mine up to the town borders and says it complies with its environmental plans. But residents say it’s unbearable to live so close to mining machines that crunch till 10 at night and start up at sunrise. MACFARLANE LINK: With the mining operations getting closer and closer to the people’s homes, there aren’t many options for the people of Ogies in Mpumalanga. It’s either they move, or fight… but moving without compensation is not an option, so the fight is on. ZEHIR OMAR, ATTORNEY: Go to the people. Pay them fair compensation and talk to them with the aim of moving. This is expropriation using coercion through mining. ADRIAAN MULLER, GUESTHOUSE AND CRÈCHE OWNER: Buy us out, we go. Otherwise, we’re going to stop Glencore’s new operations, we’re going to stop them. VO: Glencore insists it’s compliant on every level. Locals say Glencore just ticks legal boxes without meaningful engagement or building a mutually beneficial relationship with them. JOSEPH ZIKHALI, RESIDENT: We keep on fighting with this Glencore. The main thing it’s the production. They don’t worry about our lives. VO: Feeling the mine disregards them, Zikhali and some of his supporters marched to the mine and handed a memorandum of grievances to management in February. Steven Mhlanga joined that march. MACFARLANE MOLELI: Is there absolutely no engagement happening between you and the mine to try and resolve these issues? STEVEN MHLANGA, RESIDENT: There are forums, but it’s a lip service that they give to us. They just want to come there and just speak and speak, but nothing happens. It’s … no results. VO: Mhlanga, like many locals, used to live on farms that were taken over by the mines. Mhlanga and his grandparents were relocated to Phola, a township to the north of Ogies, three years ago. STEVEN MHLANGA, RESIDENT: There’s other cracks this side. This solar is not working. VO: Like many others, Mhlanga feels they got tiny, shoddily built houses and empty promises. STEVEN MHLANGA, RESIDENT: Here we’re just suffering more. They just brought us more, more, more deep into poverty. VO: Glencore says building inspectors signed off on all the houses they built. Without ESKOM power to the area, Glencore says each house has a solar geyser and gas stove; plus municipal water and rainwater tanks. Protesters feel the mine made empty promises to get the community’s support. JOSEPH ZIKHALI, RESIDENT: In the memorandum we mention quite of things, the skills development, because our community they are not working in this mine. Our town -- you can see how many potholes are here, we can’t do nothing, because we don’t have nothing. Glencore is here, they don’t help us with nothing. VO: Glencore says most of the mine’s employees live within 50 km of the mine and they prioritise hiring locals. About 18% are from Ogies and Phola and 67% from Emalahleni, 40 km away. MACFARLANE MOLELI: So you people are ready to work, you just want opportunities? STEVEN MHLANGA, RESIDENT: We want opportunities and then make our lives better. VO: Glencore hit back at protesters, getting an urgent interdict to stop the group from obstructing the mine’s business. It said they caused “irreparable harm” when they blocked the mine entrance and threw stones. Zikhali’s due back in court in May to say why the interdict should not be made permanent. VO: In January Glencore suffered a blow in the Land Claims Court when it tried to urgently evict the last few families from GGV Village to Phola. The land now belongs to the mine but the people have lived there for decades. ZEHIR OMAR, ATTORNEY: How do you order a whole community living in a rural community to supplant themselves into an urban setup? It’s a small matchbox house. You are imposing a huge trauma on men, women and children. VO: The families say they will go if Glencore buys them a similar plot. The Land Claims Court agreed it was dangerous to live so close to mining, but Glencore must go through the usual legal eviction process in terms of the Extension of Security of Tenure Act. MACFARLANE LINK: The people of this village have won the battle to stay here for now. They refused to relocate to a township -- a life to which they are not accustomed. But how long can they hold onto their property with mining operations just at their doorstep? VO: Glencore says it now uses electronic blasting, which limits noise and ground vibration. But residents say it does little to alleviate the noise of machinery and dust. ANNE-MARIE MULLER, SECRETARY: DISTRESSED MINING COMMUNITY OF OGIES FORUM: ...it does affect you, because some of the people, they start complaining, they’re got running noses, they got headaches... There’s children staying here that some medical reports says it’s air pollution that they got this allergic to the eyes, to the nose, kept with… they’ve got… they’re constantly sick. The mine says there is nothing that can make you sick. VO: The residents’ forum now waits for a court date to present their complaints to a judge. PROMOS 10 secs VO: It’s high noon in Ogies in Mpumalanga, as residents resort to violent protest and court action to battle the coal mining encroaching on their town. 15 secs VO: Digging in their heels to preserve their way of life, a small community in Mpumalanga is taking on a coal mining giant. How long can they hold out? ZEHIR OMAR, ATTORNEY: How do you order a whole community living in a rural community to supplant themselves into an urban setup? 15 secs VO: With the dust and noise of coal mining operations now just a few hundred metres away from their homes, residents of Ogies in Mpumalanga are fed up. ADRIAAN MULLER: Buy us out, we go. Otherwise, we’re going to stop Glencore’s new operations, we’re going to stop them.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Despite our expose of the structural damage, noise and dust Glencore's coal mining has caused in Ogies, Glencore's operations have expanded and the residents are desperate.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: While the human rights lawyers attempt to get a court date to have the problems aired in court, it appears that Glencore has rapidly expanded their blasting on the edge of the town of Ogies -- making breathing and sleep virtually impossible. When the community protested against the dust last week -- they found themselves on the receiving end of police action. The community has been at logger heads with the mine for a long time now. As a result of many dissatisfactory engagements with some representatives of the mine, they took the step of protesting and drafting a memorandum to hand to Glencore. One of the leaders who has charges against him, Joseph Zikhali wants the community of Ogies and Phola to be the first group of people that benefit from the mining activities. “Charity must begin at home before the mine can look elsewhere. I want the charges against me to be dropped as I am not a criminal I am simply fighting for our rights. Until such time where people will be employed, compensated and benefit from the mine. We will not rest."
metadata.Summary: Many of the issues the community is protesting, have not shifted in years. The standoff with Glencore seems deeper than ever. MEMORANDUM DEMANDS: 1) Inadequate and unfair economic exclusion of the hosting community and its residents in the continued mining activities of the mine. 2) Families relocated to Makause who still do not have water and electricity supply. 3) Compensation for forced removals and the relocation of graves without following traditional customs. 4) The mine and all its major contractors to demonstrate their local employment and skills development statistics, local Small Medium and Micro-Enterprises (SMME’s) that they are developing and are currently contracted directly with the mine or any of its major contractors. Show their local socio economic development initiatives. 5) Demand that all criminal charges and the court interdict against any of their leaders resulting from their many attempts to raise their concerns be immediately withdrawn. 6) Families relocated in order to allow for mining operations to take place be compensated and collectively explore a way in which they can benefit directly in the continued mining activities.
metadata.Further information: BACKGROUND FROM PAST STORY: Guest house owners Annemarie and Mike Muller (late 50s) permanently carry around tissues -- but their constant health problems are the least of their worries -- what gets to them is that they may never get back the R6-million that they sunk into developing two guest houses in Ogies, after cashing in their pensions to invest in the town. With mines booming around the town and another application pending that will take mining to within a few hundred metres of their yard, they should have made in killing in the business guest trade. In stead the town is slowly killing them. Their home and guest houses are cracking from the constant and untimely dynamite explosions to prepare the way for mining and the heavy-duty dragline crunches away day and night, disturbing the rest of residents and visitors. A thick layer of black dust hangs in the air all the time. The people of Ogies have roped in human rights lawyer Zehir Omar to help them fight three mines in their area (GLENCORE, ANGLO AMERICAN and SHAFT32) on human rights grounds. The DISRTESSED MINING COMMUNITY OF OGIES COMMITTEE that's been founded between the town and township, claims their right to a safe and clean environment is being destroyed, without them ever having been consulted on what was to come...now they sit with houses cracked and banks unwilling to touch the area, so they cannot sell up and leave. OGIES' LEGAL CASE: Two local doctors are willing to stick their necks out to confirm that a rising incidence of respiratory diseases in the area can be attributed to the intense pollution by coal dust. The group has had some minor success in court already this year when they managed to get a South Gauteng High Court innterdict to stop Glencore from privatising a public road for their own use...a move that would have cut off the town's access to the main school. Omar feels that the community's problems would be completely addressed and solved if only the Department of Mineral Resources would send an inspector to the area to look at the residents complaints. Having got nowhere with getting said inspector to the area, he's approached the Public Protector (that office should really be willing and able to investigate the abuse or neglect of state institutions to enforce residents' complaints)...but the Public Protector dismissed Omar and Ogies and threaten to lump them with costs, should they pursue the matter. For their part, all three mines deny any wrongdoing and have been fighting Omar in court. Glencore aims to mine an area of 113m2 for another 22 years -- it denies that it's encroaching on the town...we would have to get independent expert opinion but it certainly LOOKS to the naked eye that they're closer than the 1000m buffer zone they should be. I want to pull the focus a bit wider -- 67% of Mpumalanga is now covered by open cast coal mining -- this has cut the production of maize by a million tonnes. According to an often-quoted study by the Northwest University on behalf of West European governments that are considering whether to re-open certain mining areas in Europe, Witbank and surroundings -- up to and including areas like Ogies, are now THE most polluted in the world of any mining area that's been the subject of study. I want to investigate problems with breathing and water -- in Witbank (provincial capital, half hour away from Ogies) I have reports/case studies of black lung/mining tuberculosis in people who've never mined, but who live right next to mine dumps. This is all happening in a context where the area has already paid a heavy price for virtually unrestricted coal mining -- Anglo is paying a fortune to rehabilitate the town's drinking water and there have long been sink holes and burning earth from old and abandoned coal mines.
